Dean believes the case failed because prosecutors could not prove he physically prevented officers from their duties. After the shooter's arrest, investigators began uncovering what led to the tragedy. Three victims were tragically killed in the parking lot and five more upon entry. Unfortunately, Officer Talley was shot on entry and never recovered. He was the first Boulder officer killed in the line of duty in almost 30 years. The suspect later found and killed one person in hiding, resulting in a total of 10 victims. One hidden person, a nurse who slid onto a shelf of potato chips to hide, recognize the sound of a nearby victim taking their last breath after being discovered and shot. The gunman carried a Ruger AR-556 pistol and a 9-millimeter handgun. Though only the AR was used to fire 47 rounds, he had 10 high-capacity magazines on his person and in his vehicle. No shooting victim survived except the gunman, who was shot through one thigh by police. He bought his weapons through a website that advertises assault rifles for under $500. After purchase, they were sent to Eagle's Nest Armory, a physical third-party gun store that ran passing background checks, despite red flags that laws overlooked at the time. Months later, Colorado revised gun laws that would have prevented the purchase. The shooter's misdemeanor assault conviction three years earlier only got 18 months and was not domestic related, allowing him to bypass the law on technicalities at the time. New laws barred gun purchases for five years after any violent misdemeanor, regardless of jail time or domestic abuse prerequisites. Notably, gun stores are allegedly not shown these details when presented background results and wouldn't have known about the gunman's violent convictions. Legislators also closed the Charleston loophole, which allowed sales after three days if the government failed to return background check results. Dealers must now get Colorado Bureau of Investigation approval before any transfer. Despite the new laws, victims' families were legally blocked from seeking damages from the gun companies that enabled the purchase. This challenge stems from decades of lobbying that shields gun companies from legal liability. In 2000, a year after the Columbine shooting, Colorado legislators passed those laws and required victims' families to pay defense fees if they attempt to sue and lose. Federally, the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, passed in 2005 under President George W. Bush, further blocked lawsuits against gun companies for mass shootings. Four decades, these laws have shielded gun companies in practice. For example, in 2012, the family of Jessica Gawi killed in another Colorado shooting sued the companies that sold the shooter ammunition and tear gas. They lost the case, were ordered to pay nearly a quarter million dollars in defense fees, and eventually filed for bankruptcy after losing their daughter's life. Reports indicate that was the second mass shooting Jessica was a victim to in a matter of just five weeks. In other states, some families succeeded in suing gun companies specifically over weapon marketing. In 2022, Sandy Hook families won a $73 million settlement from Remington, claiming their marketing targeted at-risk young males. In 2023, likely inspired by the Sandy Hook case, Colorado repealed the law forcing plaintiffs to pay defense fees and passed a bill allowing victims to sue gun companies over marketing practices. Shortly after the shooting, President Biden also issued an executive order redefining firearms, though briefly reclassified as a short-barreled rifle. Ongoing debate in 2025 has allowed these weapons to remain federally classified and sold as pistols. The AR-556 used in the attack is marketed as a pistol, despite being nearly identical to the AR-15 and using the same ammunition. After the brief change in law, victims' families sued Sturm, Ruger and Company, claiming it marketed the AR-556 pistol recklessly by glorifying its killing power and promoting it to lone gunmen. The suit notes the company first advertised it as a rifle in 24. then rebranded a variant as a pistol in 2019 to bypass regulations, enabling the shooter to buy it without added restrictions. Investigations revealed the gunman purchased the weapon just six days prior to the shooting, a process that would have taken months if the weapon was classified as a rifle. The civil lawsuit is still ongoing, as U.S. legislators continue to deliberate the gun's legal definition, meaning this court case will likely result in a years-long legal battle. Fifty-nine-year-old Suzanne Fountain, a shopper, an active member of the Boulder and Denver theater community. 61-year-old Kevin Mahoney, a shopper who had recently attended his daughter's wedding. She described him as a man of love and light. 62-year-old Lynn Murray, an Instacart worker, and retired photo editor for glamour, Marie Claire and Cosmopolitan. 65-year-old Jody Waters, a shopper who owned and worked at boutiques on Boulder's Pearl Street Mall, and 51-year-old officer Eric Talley, the first officer to enter the store. behind a wife and seven children.
